agree.reason: The plain admission that A1C results can't be promised would earn some trust from a wary reader, and the $59 no-commitment trial is an easy step, but nothing speaks to why this reader would stick with it past two months when they quit everything else.

honest.reason: It drops the A1C promise and gives all 14 results, including the one that went up, but it adds an unsupported claim ('I don't use a template or an algorithm'), slightly overstates with 'you don't have to count', and leaves out that medication changes weren't tracked.

works_the_facts.reason: It works out $12.90 a meal but never turns 37 of 88 into a share (42% staying more than six months), which is the figure that would matter most to someone who has quit within two months before, and it drops the 0.6-point average without explaining why.

right_comparison.reason: It describes the daily work of counting and cooking alone, but it never compares itself with the apps and delivery service this reader already tried and dropped.

qualification.reason: The A1C hedge is tied to real numbers and gives a reason the results can't be generalised, but it gives the reader nothing they can check for themselves, such as what result to look for after three months.

objections.reason: It meets the fear of commitment and of health hype, but it leaves out the 15-minute call with the dietitian and the 4-week menu rotation, both of which would answer the objection 'I'll quit again' or 'I'll get bored.'

fit.reason: It is a clear sales page of about 400 words with headings and a single trial button, as the brief asked.
